title: Why Are Fetch Quests Boring? | Designing Meaningful Quests

scenes.title: Read the Actions Inside an Errand
lines: Bring back three items. It is a familiar request in games.
Some errands make you curious about the next destination,
while others just make you want to finish.
The difference may lie in what happens between the instruction and delivery.
We will compare travel and gathering in Skyrim with resource exploration in Subnautica,
then change conditions in an original delivery prototype.
We will examine three questions.
What choices happen along the way? What changes after delivery?
And does the return journey offer anything new?

scenes.title: 작은 부탁과 탐험을 이어 보기
lines: On the beach in A Short Hike, another hiker asks for shells.
Watch the request and the character walking back into the surroundings.
Writing only the item name can leave out the exploration in between.
Looking nearby, climbing a hill and meeting someone become part of the trip.
We are looking for actions to choose, beyond whether a marker exists.
Visible paths and changes in height provide information for movement.
Every trip does not need to become a difficult challenge.
Find one place where a small request meets the existing exploration.
The three earlier questions help us identify and record these real actions.

scenes.title: Choices Along the Way
lines: First, look at the actions on the way, rather than only the destination.
When gathering materials in Subnautica, you inspect your surroundings
and use the remaining oxygen to decide whether to keep searching or surface.
This is not a quest assigned by a character,
but an example of a player seeking materials for their own needs.
A gathering goal can contain observation and decisions.
If following a marker leaves no action or route to choose,
extra travel time may add waiting rather than meaningful activity.
Write down the moments when players make decisions during your quest.
Check whether those choices actually exist between destinations.

scenes.title: 등반과 활공 사이의 선택
lines: While climbing, we can see height and the remaining feathers together.
There can be a moment to consider continuing upward or taking another direction.
Here, observe the position reached and the change in the feather indicator.
When the scene shifts to gliding, the route no longer follows only ground paths.
The hills and waterfront below become possible places to land.
Walking and flying involve different movements, even toward a similar destination.
These excerpts are not a numeric experiment ranking the routes for fun.
Look for choices that the movement method leaves in your own quest.
Decisions along the way turn the time between destinations into play.

scenes.title: Changes After Completion
lines: Next, examine what changes when the task is completed.
Here are travel and mining scenes from Skyrim.
This footage does not demonstrate the reward of a particular quest.
It illustrates the actions of travel and gathering.
The question for our own game is separate.
After delivering the items, does only the score increase?
Or does a route open, or someone behave differently?
A numerical reward can matter, but a visible consequence
may help players understand why the task mattered.
We will build that difference in a small delivery game.

scenes.title: 얻은 것이 다음 행동에 남는가
lines: Watch the compass acquisition message that appears after a conversation.
Receiving the item is clearly observable on the screen.
The next question is how that item might be used afterward.
In the earlier bridge test, completion changed where we could walk.
For an item, record what information or actions may be available in the next search.
Separate opening a treasure chest from the movement that follows the acquisition.
Spiritfarer shows gathering and material processing as other linked actions.
Think beyond the goal of collecting an item to its later use.
Check the acquisition number and the change in the next action separately.

scenes.title: Same Delivery, Different World State
lines: Both versions ask you to collect three logs along the same route and return.
Movement speed, item positions, and the score reward are identical.
In the first version, delivery raises the score and completes the request.
In the second, the same delivery repairs a broken bridge.
The places you can reach afterward actually change.
The bridge is more than decorative completion artwork.
A blocked collision area opens, allowing the character to cross.
This comparison demonstrates a change in the world state.
Whether the second version is more enjoyable still needs human playtesting.
A successful automated input trace is not an enjoyment rating.

scenes.title: 재료를 쓰는 행동과 화면의 변화
lines: In Spiritfarer, moving around the ship brings us to different work areas.
Watch material handling and caring for passengers in sequence.
Both involve an interaction, but their visible results differ.
For materials, observe what is processed; for care, observe who responds.
Our earlier test changed only the bridge state after the same wood delivery.
These different game excerpts are not two versions of that controlled comparison.
They help us look for the target and next action connected by a request.
We can record a usable item or a relationship response as well as an opening door.
Show the completion message together with the result that remains.

scenes.title: Redesign the Return Journey
lines: Now examine the return journey.
You initially take a detour, but repairing the bridge opens a shorter route.
The same location now has a different role.
Another test adds a gate on the short route that requires an empty inventory.
You choose between returning quickly and carrying the item along the longer route.
The presence of a shortcut alone does not create a decision.
Players need to understand what they gain and give up.
You do not need an event during every moment of travel.
Quiet time can allow players to notice the surroundings or reflect.
First decide what purpose a repeated stretch should serve.

scenes.title: 돌아가는 이동을 새로 읽기
lines: Return to the gliding and return travel in A Short Hike.
Coming down from a high place shows familiar scenery from another direction.
A place seen earlier may provide a clue for choosing where to go next.
Our original test changed the return route through the bridge and inventory conditions.
In the real example, observe where the character looks and moves downward.
This does not mean adding a new enemy or event to every return trip.
Spiritfarer also shows movement around the ship between work areas and passengers.
Decide whether the end of a trip leads to another task or leaves room to rest.
The same place can be revisited with a different goal and different information.

scenes.title: Test the Play with Three Questions
lines: When designing a quest, add three lines beneath its objective.
List choices on the way, changes after the task, and new information on return.
If all three are empty, before adding more requests,
introduce a small change in one stretch of the journey.
Ask players where they paused and which route they chose.
Check what they thought changed after completion.
Their understanding may differ from your design intent.
The number of items alone does not determine a good errand.
Examine the decisions players make inside a small request
alongside the changes those decisions leave behind.

scenes.title: 부탁 하나를 세 구간으로 기록하기
lines: Finally, record one request from real scenes in three parts.
First, note the route and action chosen after hearing the request and setting out.
Next, note the visible result of finding or using an item.
Last, note the new place or next task noticed while returning.
A record of character movement differs from evidence that a player understood it.
Ask someone who played which choices and changes they remember.
If those are unclear, inspect the delivery scene before increasing the item count.
Add one observed action and result to each of the three earlier questions.
A small errand becomes material for designing the play in between.
